# The Weight of Memory

Rajesh sits in the warehouse office during his lunch break, though he rarely eats anymore. At seventy-nine, he still works part-time in the distribution center where he's been employed for the last fifteen years—a steady job that keeps him occupied, keeps him moving. He unwraps the same sandwich his ex-wife used to pack for him, a habit he never broke even after the divorce. He takes one bite and sets it aside.

The fluorescent lights hum overhead, and Rajesh's jaw tightens. That sound—the constant electrical buzz—reminds him of something he cannot quite name, though his body knows exactly what it is. His hands begin to shake slightly, and he grips the edge of the desk. He closes his eyes and counts backward from ten, a technique his daughter taught him years ago when she finally asked him why he flinched at the sound of car backfires.

Sixty-four years have passed since he served in the military, since the night his unit came under heavy fire during a border skirmish. He was twenty-three then, strong and certain. He remembers the sound—a roaring that seemed to come from everywhere at once—and the weight of his friend Arun's body when he dragged him to cover. Arun didn't survive. Rajesh did, and he has never fully understood why that division of fate fell the way it did.

For decades, Rajesh told himself the memories had faded. He worked, he married, he raised two children. He drank more than he should have, especially in the evenings, but he functioned. When his wife finally left him fifteen years ago, she said she couldn't bear living with a ghost anymore. He didn't argue. He moved into a small apartment and took the warehouse job.

But the memories haven't faded. They've only become more vivid as he's aged, as if his mind has finally decided he has enough time left to process what he spent decades trying to outrun. He wakes at three in the morning, drenched in sweat, uncertain whether the sounds he's hearing are real or remnants of that long-ago night. He avoids crowded spaces now—the shopping mall terrifies him, the way bodies move unpredictably through space. He's stopped attending his grandson's school events because he cannot sit in an auditorium without his heart racing, without feeling the walls closing in.

The warehouse work suits him because it's repetitive and solitary. He moves boxes, checks inventory, organizes shipments. The physical work keeps his mind occupied during the day, though even here, unexpected sounds startle him—a forklift beeping, a metal shelf clattering—and his colleagues have learned not to approach him from behind.

At night, in his apartment, he watches the same old Bollywood films he watched as a young man, seeking comfort in the familiar songs and stories. But even these bring their own kind of pain. He thinks of the life he might have lived if Arun had lived, if he hadn't come home changed, if his hands didn't still tremble when he's tired.

His daughter calls once a week. She worries about him, though she doesn't say it directly. She asks if he's sleeping, if he's eating, if he's thought about talking to someone. He tells her yes to all of these questions, though only the first is sometimes true. He doesn't know how to explain to her that some things, once broken, don't fully repair—they just become part of you, a weight you learn to carry differently as you grow older.
